title: Big O
objectives: Classify running times with big O and compare growth rates.

screens.title: Six ways to grow
screens.prose:
Each curve is the step count of an algorithm as the input size $n$ grows. The y axis is a log scale: each gridline is ten times the one below.

Slide $n$ and watch $n^2$ and $2^n$.
screens.question: From which $n$ on is $2^n$ bigger than $n^2$ for good?

widget.label: Smallest n
widget.accept: 5: at $n = 4$ both are 16, and from 5 on $2^n$ stays ahead.

hints.text: Slide $n$ one step at a time and compare the two numbers in the caption.
At $n = 4$ the two points sit on top of each other.
$n = 3$: 9 against 8. $n = 4$: 16 against 16. $n = 5$: 25 against 32, and $2^n$ doubles each step after that.

feedback.correct: From $n = 5$, $2^n$ is ahead and stays ahead.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the last $n$ where $n^2$ is at least $2^n$, then go one further.

byKey.one: At $n = 1$, $2^n$ is ahead, but $n^2$ catches up: at $n = 3$ it is 9 against 8.
byKey.tie: At $n = 4$ they are equal, 16 each. Bigger means strictly ahead, which starts at 5.
byKey.two: At $n = 2$ they tie at 4, and at $n = 3$, $n^2$ is ahead again.

explain.text: For small $n$ the order of the curves can swap. From $n = 5$ on, $2^n$ doubles each step while $n^2$ grows by less, so it never catches up. What matters is the order for **large** $n$: $1, \log n, n, n \log n, n^2, 2^n$.

screens.title: Bounded by a multiple
screens.prose: An algorithm takes $3n^2 + 50n + 7$ steps. For small $n$ the $50n$ term dominates. Compare it with $4n^2$, a constant times $n^2$.
screens.question: From which whole $n$ on is $3n^2 + 50n + 7$ below $4n^2$?

widget.label: Smallest n
widget.accept: 51: at 50 the cost is 10,007 against 10,000; at 51 it is 10,360 against 10,404.

hints.text: Slide $n$ until the two numbers in the caption swap order.
The curves cross near $n = 50$. Check both sides of it.
$4n^2$ wins when $n^2 > 50n + 7$, so when $n > 50.14$. The first whole number is 51.

feedback.correct: From $n = 51$ on, the cost stays below $4n^2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the caption either side of the crossing.

byKey.fifty: At $n = 50$ the cost is 10,007 and $4n^2$ is 10,000: still 7 above.
byKey.seventeen: That is where $3n^2$ alone passes $50n$. The question compares the whole cost with $4n^2$.
byKey.zero: At $n = 0$ the cost is 7 and $4n^2$ is 0, so the cost is above.

explain.text: From $n = 51$ on, the cost is at most $4 \times n^2$. That is what $3n^2 + 50n + 7 = O(n^2)$ says: for large $n$, the cost is bounded above by a constant times $n^2$. **Big O** keeps the fastest-growing term and drops its constant.

screens.title: Classify the snippets
screens.prose: Each snippet runs on a list `prices` of length `n`. Count how its steps grow, then keep only the growth. Type the class: `O(1)`, `O(log n)`, `O(n)`, `O(n log n)`, `O(n^2)` or `O(2^n)`.

params.title: Five snippets
lines: for p in prices: total += p
for q in prices: diffs.append(p - q)

screens.question: Fill in the class of each snippet.

hints.text: For each snippet, ask how many times its innermost line runs.
D halves `n` each time round. How many halvings take $n$ down to 1?
A: once. B: $n$ times. C: $n \times n$. D: about $\log_2 n$ halvings. E: $n$ outer runs of a $\log_2 n$ inner loop.

feedback.correct: A $O(1)$, B $O(n)$, C $O(n^2)$, D $O(\log n)$, E $O(n \log n)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how often the innermost line runs in each snippet.

byKey.r2c1: Snippet C runs its inner line for every `p` and every `q`: $n \times n$ times.
byKey.r3c1: Snippet D halves `n` each time. Going from $n$ to 1 takes about $\log_2 n$ halvings, not $n$ steps.
byKey.r4c1: Snippet E runs a doubling loop of about $\log_2 n$ steps once per price: $n \log n$ in all.

explain.text: You counted how often the innermost line runs. Halving or doubling up to $n$ takes about $\log_2 n$ steps, so D is $O(\log n)$. Snippet E nests that inside a loop over $n$, giving $O(n \log n)$.

screens.title: Double the input
screens.prose: Four step counts at $n = 1{,}024$, which is $2^{10}$. The input doubles to $2{,}048$, the dashed line on the right.
screens.question: Fill in the step counts at $n = 2{,}048$.

hints.text: Multiply each entry out with $n = 2{,}048$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work each row out at $n = 2{,}048$.

byKey.r2c2: $n \log_2 n$ at 2,048 is $2{,}048 \times 11$. Both factors change.

explain.text: Doubling $n$ adds a constant (1) to $\log n$, doubles $n$, slightly more than doubles $n \log n$ (2.2 times), and quadruples $n^2$. So a doubling test tells you the class: time it at $n$ and $2n$ and read the ratio.

screens.title: Is linear always faster?
screens.prose: Method A is $O(n)$ but does 50 steps per price: $50n$. Method B is $O(n^2)$ with one step per pair: $n^2$. Today's list has $n = 20$ prices.
screens.question: Which method does fewer steps for $n = 20$?

options.why: You read big O as a ranking at every $n$. It only describes growth for large $n$; at 20, $50n$ is 1,000 and $n^2$ is 400.
They tie at $n = 50$, where $50n = n^2 = 2{,}500$. At 20 they differ.

options.text: We cannot tell without timing them

hints.text: Put $n = 20$ into both step counts.
At the dashed line, which curve is lower?

feedback.correct: B wins at 20; A wins from $n = 51$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two counts at $n = 20$.

byKey.a: You read $O(n)$ as faster at every size. Big O hides the constant 50, and below $n = 50$ that constant makes A the slower method.

explain.text: Big O describes growth, not the exact cost. Below $n = 50$ the constant 50 makes A the slower method. Past 50, $n^2$ grows faster and B loses for good.

screens.title: Constant is not cheap
screens.prose: A risk check always does exactly 1,000,000 steps, whatever the size of the book. A plain scan of the book does $3n$ steps.
screens.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: The check is $O(1)$, yet at $n = 1{,}000$ it costs far more than the scan
The check is not $O(1)$, because a million steps is a lot
options.why: $O(1)$ means bounded by a constant, however large. A million that never grows is a constant.

options.text: The check is $O(1)$, so it is cheaper than the scan for every $n$
options.why: Bounded is not small: the scan costs less until $3n$ passes $10^6$, at about $n = 333{,}334$.

options.text: Both are $O(1)$ for a fixed book
options.why: For a fixed book everything is a constant. Big O asks how the cost grows as $n$ grows.

hints.text: What does $O(1)$ promise: small, or bounded?
At $n = 1{,}000$ the scan does 3,000 steps.
The check is always $10^6$, so it is $O(1)$. The scan passes it only when $3n > 10^6$, at $n \approx 333{,}334$.

feedback.correct: Constant time means bounded, not fast.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate two questions: does the cost grow with $n$, and how big is it?

byKey.always: You read $O(1)$ as cheap. It means the cost never grows; here it is stuck at a million.

explain.text: $O(1)$ only says the cost does not grow with $n$. This one is stuck at a million steps, so the scan is cheaper for any book under 333,334 positions. Big O compares growth; the constants still decide small cases.

screens.prose:
$f(n) = O(g(n))$ means: there are constants $c$ and $n_0$ with

$$f(n) \le c \, g(n) \quad \text{for every } n \ge n_0.$$

In practice, keep the fastest-growing term and drop its constant. From slowest to fastest: $1, \log n, n, n \log n, n^2, 2^n$.
screens.question: What is $2n \log n + 40n + 9$ in big O?

options.why: You kept the term with the biggest coefficient, $40n$. For large $n$, $n \log n$ outgrows any constant times $n$.
That is right but not simplified: big O drops the constant 2.
You multiplied the terms. A sum grows like its fastest term.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which term grows fastest as $n$ grows?

explain.text: $\log n$ grows without limit, so $2n \log n$ eventually passes $40n$ (once $\log_2 n > 20$). Drop the 2 and the slower terms: $O(n \log n)$.

screens.title: Proving a bound
screens.prose: We show that $3n^2 + 50n + 7 = O(n^2)$ by finding $c$ and $n_0$. Each line needs a reason.
screens.question: Put the lines of the proof in order.

lines.text: So $c = 60$ and $n_0 = 1$ meet the definition: $3n^2 + 50n + 7 = O(n^2)$.

hints.text: Bound each lower term by a multiple of $n^2$ first.
The two bounds on $50n$ and $7$ can come in either order.
Bound $50n$ and $7$, add the bounds to $3n^2$, then read off $c$ and $n_0$.

feedback.correct: A different $c$ from the slider's 4, and just as valid.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You can only add the bounds once you have them.

byKey.done: The conclusion names $c$ and $n_0$, so it comes last.

explain.text: Each lower term is at most a multiple of $n^2$ once $n \ge 1$. Adding gives $c = 60$ with $n_0 = 1$. On the slider you found $c = 4$ with $n_0 = 51$: any working pair proves the bound.

screens.title: Count, then choose
screens.prose: Method A loops once over $n$ prices and does 50 steps per price. Method B loops over every price inside a loop over every price, one step each. Count the steps with counters, not a clock, so the answer is the same on every machine.
screens.question: Write `steps_a(n)`, `steps_b(n)` and `cheaper(n)`, which returns `"A"`, `"B"` or `"tie"`.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests: the two step counts, then `cheaper` for $n$ from 0 to 1,000, including the tie at 50.

hints.text: Each function can count with a loop and `steps += ...`.
The curves cross at $n = 50$, where both counts are 2,500.
`steps_a` adds 50 per price; `steps_b` adds 1 in a nested loop. In `cheaper`, compare the two counts with `<`, and return `"tie"` when neither is smaller.

feedback.correct: B for small lists, a tie at 50, and A from 51 on.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-6: Test 6 expects `'tie'` at $n = 50$, where both counts are 2,500. Check equality before picking a winner.
byKey.test-10: Test 10 expects `'tie'` for $n = 0$: both methods do 0 steps on an empty list.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 expects `'B'` at $n = 10$: 100 steps against 500. The $O(n)$ method is not always cheaper.

explain.text: Your counters show the crossover the plane showed: B is cheaper below 50, A above. Counting steps gives the same answer on every machine. At $n = 0$ both do nothing, so they tie.

screens.title: A backtest loop
screens.prose: A backtest updates a position for every stock on every day: 20 years of 250 trading days is 5,000 days, across 500 stocks.
screens.question: How many times does `update` run?

hints.text: For each day, the inner loop runs once per stock.
Line 3 runs inside both loops.

feedback.correct: 2.5 million calls: fine for a nightly run.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Nested loops multiply their sizes.

byKey.added: You added the loop sizes. The stock loop runs again on every day, so they multiply.
byKey.squared: That is a triple loop, $5{,}000 \times 500 \times 500$. This code has two loops.

explain.text: $5{,}000 \times 500 = 2.5$ million calls is fine. Add a loop over every other stock inside and it becomes $1.25 \times 10^9$, 500 times more. Rewriting the double loop in pandas runs the same $O(\text{days} \times \text{stocks})$ work in C: a smaller constant, the same class.

ideas: $f(n) = O(g(n))$ means $f(n) \le c \, g(n)$ for all large $n$: an upper bound on growth, not an exact time.
Keep the fastest-growing term and drop constants: $3n^2 + 50n + 7 = O(n^2)$. The order is $1, \log n, n, n \log n, n^2, 2^n$.
Doubling $n$ adds a constant to $O(\log n)$, doubles $O(n)$ and quadruples $O(n^2)$.

formula.name: Big O
formula.tex: f(n) = O(g(n)) \iff f(n) \le c\,g(n) \text{ for all } n \ge n_0
formula.note: Some constant $c$ and starting point $n_0$ must exist.

summary.trap: $O(n)$ is not faster than $O(n^2)$ at every size: with $50n$ against $n^2$, the quadratic method wins below $n = 50$.

quiz.question: What is this in big O, with $n$ the length of `prices`?

options.why: You saw two nested loops. The inner one always runs 5 times, whatever $n$ is, so the total is $5n$.
The outer loop grows with the list, so the cost does too.
Big O drops constants: $5n$ and $n$ are the same class.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which loop grows with $n$?

explain.text: Only the outer loop depends on $n$. The inner loop is a constant 5, so the total is $5n$, which is $O(n)$.

quiz.prose: You rewrite a Python double loop over days and stocks as one pandas expression. It now runs 60 times faster.
quiz.question: What did vectorising change?

options.text: The constant: the same $O(\text{days} \times \text{stocks})$ work, done in C

options.why: pandas still touches every value once. The work still grows with days times stocks.

options.text: The class: it is now $O(\log n)$
options.why: Nothing halves the data. Each value is still processed.

options.text: Nothing, so the timing must be wrong
options.why: Constants matter in practice. A 60-fold faster inner step is real.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Does pandas skip any of the values?

explain.text: Vectorising moves the loop into compiled code, so each step is much cheaper. Every value is still visited, so doubling the data still doubles the time.

quiz.prose: An $O(n^2)$ pairs report takes 4 minutes on 10,000 rows.
quiz.question: Roughly how long should it take on 20,000 rows?

options.why: You doubled the time, as for $O(n)$. Doubling $n$ multiplies $n^2$ by 4.
Big O does not fix the time; it says how the time grows with $n$.
That multiplies by $4^2$. One doubling of $n$ multiplies $n^2$ by $2^2 = 4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What happens to $n^2$ when $n$ doubles?

explain.text: $(2n)^2 = 4n^2$, so the time multiplies by 4: about 16 minutes. If it took 8, the code would be $O(n)$.

quiz.prose: A loop halves the search range each step. It takes 20 steps for 1,000,000 sorted prices.
quiz.question: About how many steps for 2,000,000 prices?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many halvings turn 2,000,000 into 1,000,000?

byKey.double: You doubled the steps, as for $O(n)$. For $O(\log n)$ doubling $n$ adds a constant: one halving.
byKey.same: Doubling $n$ does add something: one extra halving to get back to 1,000,000.

explain.text: The first halving takes 2,000,000 down to 1,000,000, and from there it is the old 20 steps. Doubling $n$ adds 1 to $\log_2 n$.
